name: Grade 8
theme: The Church through history, and preparing for Confirmation

lessons.title: Jesus founds the Church
lessons.idea: Jesus founded one Church on Peter and the apostles. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confessed him as the Christ, and Jesus gave him the keys of the kingdom. That office continues in the Pope and the bishops.
lessons.question: Why Peter?
lessons.activity: “Keys and rock” study (30 min). Annotate Matthew 16:13–19 with Isaiah 22:20–22 (the royal steward’s key) and John 21:15–17 (“Feed my sheep”). Students record what authority Jesus gives and how the apostolic office continues (bishops as successors, Pope as successor of Peter).
teach: Jesus founded the Church by preaching the Kingdom, choosing the Twelve and giving Peter a unique role (CCC 551–553, 765). The Church was “born” from the pierced side of Christ and manifested at Pentecost (CCC 766).
The keys signify authority to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19; Isaiah 22). The same power is shared with the apostles (Matthew 18:18) and Peter is always first in the lists (CCC 552).
Apostolic succession passes the apostles’ mission to bishops through laying on of hands (CCC 861–862). The Pope, as Peter’s successor, is the visible principle of unity (CCC 882).
Early witnesses such as Clement of Rome (c. 96) and Irenaeus (c. 180) point to Rome’s special authority. Present these respectfully.
talk: How do we see succession today?
quiz: Jesus built his Church on…|Peter|Paul|Judas|Herod|0|Matthew 16:18.
The keys signify…|Locks|Authority|Silence|Wealth|1|Isaiah 22:22.
Peter’s successor is…|The king|The prior|The emperor|The Pope|3|CCC 882.
lessons.life: Learn the name of the Pope and the line of succession.
lessons.saint: Peter: a fisherman who denied Jesus and was forgiven, and became the first pope.
misc: “Jesus never intended an institutional Church.”
“Peter was just the first among equals with no special role.”
lessons.mem: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
lessons.hook: Show a ring of keys and ask: “What does the person who holds the keys do?” Read Matthew 16:13–19 and note the question Jesus asks first: “Who do you say that I am?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the keys, the rock and apostolic succession in a short paragraph.

lessons.title: The Church as mystery, sacrament, body
lessons.idea: The Church is a mystery that cannot be exhausted by one image. She is the sacrament of salvation, the Body of Christ, the People of God, the Temple of the Spirit and the Bride of Christ. Each image shows something true.
lessons.question: Which image helps you?
lessons.activity: “Illustrate three images” (30 min). Students choose three images from CCC 753–757 (flock, vineyard, building, bride), read Ephesians 1:22–23 and 5:25–32, and make a poster that pairs a drawing with a short explanation and a verse.
teach: The Church is a “mystery” — a visible society and a spiritual reality (CCC 770–771). She is “the universal sacrament of salvation” (CCC 774–776).

The Body of Christ: Christ is the head, we are members (Ephesians 1:22–23; CCC 787–795). The People of God: a priestly, prophetic and royal people (CCC 781–786). The Temple of the Spirit (CCC 797–798).
The Bride of Christ (Ephesians 5:25–32): Christ loves and gives himself for her (CCC 796). This shows both tenderness and fidelity.
Vatican II (Lumen Gentium) uses these images. Acknowledge that the Church’s members are sinners (CCC 827).
talk: How is the Church both human and divine?
quiz: The Church is called the Body of…|Mary|Peter|Paul|Christ|3|CCC 779.
The Church is also the…|Servant of kings|Mother of all|Queen of earth|Bride of Christ|3|CCC 796.
Lumen Gentium is a…|Council of Trent|Encyclical of Leo XIII|Vatican II document|Hymn|2|CCC 748.
lessons.life: Read Lumen Gentium chapter 1.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: a lay Dominican who counseled popes and loved the Church while calling for reform.
misc: “The Church is just a human organization.”
“The Church is only the clergy.”
lessons.mem: “He has put all things under his feet and has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body.” (Ephesians 1:22–23)
lessons.hook: Put students in groups and give each one an image (body, people, bride, temple). Ask: “What does this image say about our relationship to Christ and to each other?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain three images of the Church and what each teaches.

lessons.title: Marks of the Church
lessons.idea: The four marks of the Church — one, holy, catholic and apostolic — are named in the Nicene Creed. They are gifts of Christ and also tasks for believers. Each is real, though imperfectly lived.
lessons.question: How does each mark appear today?
lessons.activity: “Marks and evidence” (30 min). Students take each mark and give biblical grounds, historical evidence and a present-day example (one: Ephesians 4:4–6, the Mass worldwide; holy: saints; catholic: 1.3 billion on every continent; apostolic: unbroken lines of bishops). Debate: how do wounds to unity challenge the first mark?
teach: One: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism (CCC 813–822). Unity is a gift; divisions among Christians are a wound. The Church works for Christian unity (ecumenism, CCC 820–822).
Holy: because Christ sanctifies her through sacraments and the Spirit (CCC 823–829). The Church has saints in every age and sinners too.

Catholic: “according to the whole”: the fullness of faith and means of salvation, and sent to all people (CCC 830–856). Apostolic: founded on the apostles, teaching their doctrine and governed by their successors (CCC 857–865).
Teach respectfully about other Christians, who share Baptism and many truths (CCC 818–819).
talk: How does each mark show up?
quiz: Unity includes…|One language|One faith, worship, governance|One building|One culture|1|CCC 815.
Catholicity means…|Roman|Local|Fullness and universality|Large|2|CCC 830.
Apostolicity means…|Eastern|Quick|Founded on the apostles|Ancient|2|CCC 857.
lessons.life: Pray for unity among Christians.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Antioch: a bishop who was thrown to the lions in Rome and wrote letters on the Eucharist and the Church.
misc: “If the Church is holy, no one in it can be bad.”
“Catholic means ‘Roman’ and nothing more.”
lessons.mem: “There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of us all.” (Ephesians 4:4–6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How would you identify a particular school?” (name, uniform, motto). Introduce the marks as the Church’s identifying signs.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four marks, explain each and give one sign that it is real today.

lessons.title: Persecution and martyrs
lessons.idea: The first three centuries were years of persecution. Martyrs such as Stephen, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, Perpetua and Felicity bore witness to Christ with their lives. “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of Christians.”
lessons.question: What is a witness?
lessons.activity: “Martyr profiles” (30 min). Groups read short excerpts from the Martyrdom of Polycarp and the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, then make a profile card: who, when, charge, their words, what they teach us. Present, then discuss modern martyrdom today.
teach: The word “martyr” means “witness” (CCC 2473). Martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of faith (CCC 2473–2474). The Church honors martyrs as models and intercessors.
Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) wrote on the way to Rome, “Let me be food for the wild beasts.” Polycarp (c. 155) refused to deny Christ: “Eighty-six years I have served him.”
Perpetua and Felicity (203) show young women’s courage. Tertullian wrote that “the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians.”
More Christians died for the faith in the twentieth century than in all the previous centuries combined. Speak with sensitivity and hope.
quiz: Martyr means…|King|Priest|Warrior|Witness|3|CCC 2473.
Ignatius of Antioch was killed in…|Egypt|Greece|Spain|Rome|3|Tradition.
The blood of martyrs is the…|End of faith|Seed of Christians|Cost of war|Sign of defeat|1|Tertullian.
lessons.life: Pray for persecuted Christians.
lessons.saint: Perpetua and Felicity: two young mothers who were martyred in Carthage in 203 and left a diary of their faith.
misc: “Martyrs wanted to die.”
“Persecution ended with Rome.”
lessons.mem: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit… Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” (Acts 7:59–60)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 7:54–60 and ask what Stephen says as he dies. Note the echo of Jesus’ words from the Cross.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two martyrs, what they said or did and what we learn from them.

lessons.title: Constantine and the councils
lessons.idea: In 313 Constantine ended the persecution of Christians. Soon the Church faced heresies, especially about who Christ is. Councils at Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) defined the faith still professed in the Creed.
lessons.question: What did Nicaea teach?
lessons.activity: “Compare the creeds” (30 min). Place the Apostles’ Creed and the Nicene Creed side by side. Students highlight what Nicaea added (“begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father”). Then match each council with the heresy it answered: Arianism, Macedonianism, Nestorianism, Monophysitism.
teach: The Edict of Milan (313) gave Christians freedom of worship. Constantine called the Council of Nicaea (325) to settle Arius’ claim that the Son was a creature. Nicaea taught that the Son is “consubstantial” (homoousios) with the Father (CCC 465, 242).
Constantinople (381) defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit and completed the Nicene Creed. Ephesus (431) called Mary Theotokos. Chalcedon (451) taught two natures in one Person (CCC 466–469).
The Church defines doctrine to protect the faith, not to invent it (CCC 88–90). The councils worked under the Spirit with the Pope’s authority.
Constantine’s patronage helped the Church but also brought entanglement with the state. Be honest about both sides.
quiz: Nicaea defined that the Son is…|Created|Lesser|A prophet|Consubstantial with the Father|3|CCC 465.
Arius taught that Jesus was…|A creature|Man only|God|Spirit|0|CCC 465.
The Nicene Creed is said at…|Weddings only|Sunday Mass|Funerals only|Baptism only|1|CCC 195.
lessons.life: Say the Nicene Creed with attention.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: bishop of Alexandria, who defended the divinity of Christ through repeated exiles.
misc: “Constantine invented Christian doctrine at Nicaea.”
“Councils added new beliefs.”
lessons.mem: “We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, … consubstantial with the Father.” (Nicene Creed)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is Jesus a creature, or is he God?” Explain that the answer wasn’t obvious to everyone until the Church spoke clearly.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain one council, the heresy it answered and the teaching it defined.

lessons.title: The Fathers of the Church
lessons.idea: The Fathers of the Church are early teachers and bishops whose writings shaped doctrine and prayer. Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine are among them.
lessons.question: Who are they?
lessons.activity: “Read a Father” (30 min). Provide short excerpts: Athanasius (On the Incarnation 54: “He became man that we might become God”), Augustine (Confessions 1.1: “our heart is restless”), Chrysostom (Homily on Matthew). Students summarize, note the main idea, and decide what is still relevant.
teach: The Fathers were early witnesses to Tradition (CCC 11, 78, 688, 2651). Their agreement is a mark of the Church’s faith (Dei Verbum 8).

Some Fathers are Doctors of the Church. Jerome translated the Vulgate; Augustine wrote the Confessions and City of God; Athanasius defended Nicaea; John Chrysostom (“golden mouth”) preached eloquently.
They wrote Scripture commentaries, creeds and catechetical lectures. Their approach is practical, pastoral and prayerful.
Men and women: also mention women like Monica, Macrina and Perpetua, who shaped them.
quiz: The Fathers were…|Popes only|Monks only|Early Church writers|Kings|2|CCC 11.
Augustine wrote…|Imitation of Christ|Spiritual Exercises|Summa|Confessions|3|Tradition.
Jerome translated…|The Koran|The Bible into Latin|The Talmud|The Iliad|1|Tradition.
lessons.life: Read a page from a Father in the Reading room.
lessons.saint: Augustine: who searched for truth for years before writing, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
misc: “The Fathers all agreed on everything.”
“They are only for scholars.”
lessons.mem: “O God, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” (St Augustine)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who teaches the person who teaches you?” Read 2 Timothy 2:2 and talk about the chain from Paul to Timothy to others.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three Fathers, one work or idea each, and why they matter.

units.title: The Church in the Middle Ages
units.eq: What did the medieval Church achieve?

lessons.title: Monks and missionaries
lessons.idea: When persecution ended, some men and women withdrew to follow Christ more radically in prayer and work. Anthony in the Egyptian desert, Pachomius and Basil began communities; Benedict wrote a Rule built on “ora et labora” (pray and work). Monks preserved learning and carried the Gospel to new lands.
lessons.question: What did monasteries do?
lessons.activity: “A Benedictine day” (35 min). Examine the daily horarium of a monastery: Vigils, Lauds, work, lectio, Vespers, Compline. Students create a schedule that balances prayer, work and rest, and try silent lectio for five minutes.
teach: Consecrated life is a gift to the Church, a call to follow the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience (CCC 914–933). Monastic life began with Anthony of Egypt (c. 270).
Benedict’s Rule (c. 530) stresses stability, obedience, hospitality and a balanced day: “Let nothing be preferred to the work of God.” Benedictines copied manuscripts and preserved classical texts.
Missionaries such as Patrick (Ireland), Augustine of Canterbury (England), Boniface (Germany) and Cyril and Methodius (Slavs) spread the Gospel.
Monastic communities still welcome guests. Invite students to consider visiting one.
quiz: Benedict wrote a…|Hymn|Rule|Creed|Gospel|1|Tradition.
Ora et labora means…|Read and write|Pray and work|Sing and dance|Eat and sleep|1|Rule.
Monasteries preserved…|Armies|Ships|Books and learning|Taxes|2|History.
lessons.life: Try a short daily rhythm of prayer and work.
lessons.saint: Benedict: the father of Western monasticism, whose Rule says, “Prefer nothing to the work of God.”
misc: “Monks run away from the world.”
“The Middle Ages were all darkness.”
lessons.mem: “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Matthew 19:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you do with a day of silence? What would you pray for?” Read Matthew 19:21 about the rich young man.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “ora et labora” and how monks preserved the faith.

lessons.title: Cathedrals, universities and saints
lessons.idea: The Middle Ages produced great cathedrals, universities and saints. Faith shaped art, music and learning. Thomas Aquinas, Francis of Assisi, Dominic and Catherine of Siena show different ways to holiness.
lessons.question: How did faith shape culture?
lessons.activity: “Cathedral tour” (30 min). Take a virtual tour of a Gothic cathedral. Students identify the cross-shaped plan, rose window, flying buttress, stained glass stories. Then read Psalm 27:4 and write a reflection: “What do I desire from the house of the Lord?”
teach: Faith inspired beauty: the Church’s tradition holds that beauty leads to God (CCC 2500–2503). Cathedrals were “Bibles in stone and glass” for a largely illiterate people.
Universities (Paris, Bologna, Oxford) grew out of cathedral schools. Aquinas’ Summa Theologiae joined faith and reason (CCC 31–35, 159).
Francis of Assisi embraced poverty and creation; Dominic founded the Order of Preachers; Catherine of Siena counseled popes. Women such as Hildegard and Clare shaped the age.
Be honest about the flaws (wars, corruption). The era was complex, not purely golden.
quiz: Universities began in…|The 1600s|The 1900s|Ancient Rome|The Middle Ages|3|History.
Aquinas wrote…|Imitation|Summa Theologiae|Confessions|Rule|1|History.
Gothic cathedrals aim at…|Heaven|Trade|Politics|Defense|0|History.
lessons.life: Look at a cathedral and name three symbols.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
misc: “Medieval people did not think; they only prayed.”
“Cathedrals were built to show off wealth.”
lessons.mem: “One thing have I asked of the Lord, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” (Psalm 27:4)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of Chartres or Notre-Dame’s interior. Ask: “What do you notice? Why do the windows soar up?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three medieval achievements and what they show about faith and culture.

lessons.title: The East–West schism
lessons.idea: In 1054 the Churches of East and West formally divided, after centuries of growing apart. The causes included authority (the role of the Pope), the Filioque, language, culture and politics. Jesus’ prayer “that they may all be one” makes this a wound we pray to heal.
lessons.question: What caused the division?
lessons.activity: “Map the division” (30 min). Mark Rome and Constantinople, the Latin- and Greek-speaking worlds, the 1054 excommunications (Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius). List causes. Then read the 1965 lifting of excommunications (Paul VI and Athenagoras).
teach: The Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches share apostolic succession, sacraments and the Creed, but differ on papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque and other points (CCC 817–819, 838).
The sack of Constantinople by Crusaders in 1204 deepened the rift. Attempts at reunion at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439) did not last.
Today the Church seeks unity: Pope John Paul II said the Church must “breathe with both lungs.” Dialogue continues (CCC 820–822).
The 23 Eastern Catholic Churches are in full communion with Rome while keeping their own traditions.
talk: What do East and West share?
quiz: The Great Schism occurred in…|325|1517|1965|1054|3|History.
The Filioque concerns…|Icons|The Pope|Fasting|The procession of the Spirit|3|CCC 246.
Eastern Catholics are…|Protestant|Pagan|In communion with Rome|Orthodox|2|CCC 838.
lessons.life: Learn one Eastern Catholic Church’s name and customs.
lessons.saint: Cyril and Methodius: brothers who brought the Gospel to the Slavs and gave them an alphabet and a liturgy.
misc: “The East left the Church over one word.”
“Orthodox are not Christian.”
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one, even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Read John 17:20–23 and ask what Jesus prays for. Then show a map of the Roman Empire divided and ask how distance might cause misunderstanding.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the main causes of the schism and one step toward healing.

units.title: Reformation and renewal
units.eq: How did the Church respond to division?

lessons.title: The Reformation
lessons.idea: The Reformation began in 1517 when Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences. It grew into a wider break from Rome about authority, Scripture, justification and the sacraments, giving rise to Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican traditions. It left lasting wounds in Christian unity.
lessons.question: What issues divided?
lessons.activity: “Key issues chart” (30 min). Students build a chart with columns: issue, Reformers’ position, Catholic position (authority: sola scriptura vs. Scripture and Tradition; justification: faith alone vs. faith working through love; sacraments: two vs. seven; the Mass; the papacy). Include real abuses: indulgence sellers, simony, clerical corruption.
teach: The abuses were real. Many Catholics, including saints, asked for reform. Luther’s Ninety-five Theses (1517) challenged indulgence preaching (CCC 1471–1479). The break widened with the Diet of Worms (1521).

Reformers stressed Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone. Catholics affirm Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium, and justification by grace through faith that works in love (CCC 80–82, 1987–1995).
Henry VIII’s break with Rome (1534) was political. Calvin’s Geneva developed Reformed theology. Wars of religion followed.
Since Vatican II the Church recognizes our separated brothers and sisters as Christians and seeks unity (CCC 817–819).
quiz: The Reformation began in…|1054|1517|1965|325|1|History.
Luther posted…|10 Commandments|95 Theses|12 Articles|7 Sacraments|1|History.
Catholics and Protestants share…|The Mass|Papacy|Baptism and Scripture|Purgatory|2|CCC 818.
lessons.life: Pray for Christian unity.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: the lawyer and statesman who told the truth to a king and died for his conscience.
misc: “Luther simply wanted to leave the Church.”
“All Reformers agreed.”
lessons.mem: “I appeal to you, brethren… that there be no dissensions among you, but that you be united in the same mind.” (1 Corinthians 1:10)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When is it right to speak out about a problem in an institution you love? What can go wrong?” Introduce Luther as a case.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain three issues in the Reformation and how Catholics responded.

lessons.title: The Council of Trent
lessons.idea: The Council of Trent (1545–1563) responded to the Reformation by clarifying doctrine and reforming the Church. It defined the canon, the sacraments, justification and the Mass, and set up seminaries, a catechism and stricter discipline.
lessons.question: What did Trent do?
lessons.activity: “Trent summary” (30 min). Students read a summary of Trent’s decrees and sort them into doctrine and reform. Then compare the Roman Catechism (1566) to today’s Catechism of the Catholic Church. Read 2 Timothy 4:1–5.
teach: Trent affirmed seven sacraments, transubstantiation, the Mass as sacrifice and the canon of 73 books (CCC 120, 1376, 1129).
It taught justification by grace, with cooperation of the free will (CCC 2008–2010). It rejected the claim that grace is only external.
Reforms: seminaries for priests, bishops to reside in their dioceses, the Roman Catechism, a standard missal. These produced saints like Charles Borromeo.
The Counter-Reformation also brought Baroque art and new orders (Jesuits, Capuchins) and renewed missions.
quiz: Trent produced…|The Code of Canon Law|The Roman Catechism|The Summa|The Nicene Creed|1|History.
Trent required…|Seminaries|Taxes|Wars|New feasts only|0|History.
Trent responded to…|The Black Death|The Schism|The Reformation|The Crusades|2|History.
lessons.life: Read part of the Roman Catechism.
lessons.saint: Charles Borromeo: archbishop of Milan, who carried out the reforms of Trent and cared for the plague-stricken.
misc: “Trent invented new doctrines.”
“Trent was only a reaction against Protestants.”
lessons.mem: “Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season.” (2 Timothy 4:2)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If your school needed to fix problems and explain its rules, what would you do?” Compare to Trent’s doctrine and reform.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two doctrinal and two disciplinary results of Trent.

lessons.title: Missionaries and saints
lessons.idea: New religious orders and missionaries carried the Gospel across the world. Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuits; Francis Xavier traveled to India and Japan; Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross renewed the Carmelites; Francis de Sales taught holiness for everyone.
lessons.question: Who were Ignatius and Teresa?
lessons.activity: “Biography presentations” (35 min). Each student presents a 2-minute biography: Ignatius, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross, Francis de Sales, Rose of Lima, Isaac Jogues. Include a quote and a lesson for today. Link to Matthew 28:19.
teach: The Church is missionary by nature (CCC 849–856). The age of exploration brought both heroic missionaries and entanglement with colonialism; some defended native peoples (Bartolomé de las Casas).
Ignatius’ Spiritual Exercises teach discernment. Teresa and John teach contemplative prayer (CCC 2709–2719). Francis de Sales taught the “devout life” for ordinary people (CCC 2013).
Missionary martyrs include the North American Martyrs, Japanese martyrs and many in China and Africa. The Church grows by witness.
Name some saints from your own culture to show how the Gospel takes root in each people.
quiz: Ignatius founded the…|Benedictines|Jesuits|Dominicans|Franciscans|1|History.
Teresa of Avila reformed the…|Jesuits|Franciscans|Carmelites|Augustinians|2|History.
Francis Xavier went to…|Iceland|India and Japan|Egypt|Brazil only|1|History.
lessons.life: Research a missionary saint.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit missionary who carried the Gospel to India and Japan.
misc: “Missionaries were only agents of empire.”
“Only priests can be missionaries.”
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Show a world map with lines to Asia, Africa and the Americas. Ask: “What would it take to go there in 1550?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present a saint’s contribution and what it teaches today.

units.title: The modern Church
units.eq: How does the Church meet the modern world?

lessons.title: Vatican II
lessons.idea: The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965), called by John XXIII, renewed the Church’s life and mission. It issued sixteen documents, including four constitutions: on the Church (Lumen Gentium), Divine Revelation (Dei Verbum), the Liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium) and the Church in the modern world (Gaudium et Spes).
lessons.question: What changed?
lessons.activity: “Four constitutions” (35 min). Groups take one constitution, read a short excerpt and list its main ideas and a practical result (Mass in the vernacular, a call to holiness for all, Scripture’s place, dialogue with the world). Create a one-page summary and present.
teach: The Council did not change doctrine but deepened and renewed its expression (CCC 10–11). Lumen Gentium: the Church as mystery and People of God, the universal call to holiness (CCC 770–776, 2013).

Dei Verbum: Scripture and Tradition; Sacrosanctum Concilium: full, conscious, active participation in the liturgy (CCC 1071–1075). Gaudium et Spes: the Church’s joy and hope, grief and anguish for all people.
Other documents: on ecumenism (Unitatis Redintegratio), non-Christian religions (Nostra Aetate), religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae).
Be honest that interpretations differ, and encourage reading the texts themselves.
quiz: Vatican II began under…|Pius XII|John XXIII|Paul VI|Leo XIII|1|History.
Sacrosanctum Concilium concerns…|The world|The Church|The liturgy|Scripture|2|History.
Gaudium et Spes concerns…|Scripture|Liturgy|Priests|The Church in the modern world|3|History.
lessons.life: Read a short passage from Gaudium et Spes.
lessons.saint: John XXIII: the joyful pope who called the Second Vatican Council.
misc: “Vatican II abolished the old Mass or doctrine.”
“The Council changed Church teaching on everything.”
lessons.mem: “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)
lessons.hook: Say: “Open the windows,” which is what John XXIII said about the Council. Ask what that image suggests.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four constitutions and one lasting fruit of each.

lessons.title: Social teaching
lessons.idea: Catholic social teaching applies the Gospel to society. Its seven themes — dignity of the person, family and community, rights and responsibilities, option for the poor, dignity of work, solidarity, care for creation — guide how we treat people and build the common good.
lessons.question: What are the themes?
lessons.activity: “Match themes to examples” (30 min). Cards with themes and cases (a living wage, a refugee family, a polluted river, a bullied classmate, a school food drive). Students match, explain and propose a step they can take.
teach: The tradition begins with Leo XIII’s Rerum Novarum (1891) on the rights of workers and continues through Pius XI, John XXIII, Paul VI, John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis (CCC 2419–2425).
Principles: the dignity of every person (CCC 1700–1709), the common good (CCC 1905–1912), subsidiarity (CCC 1883–1885), solidarity (CCC 1939–1942), preferential love for the poor (CCC 2443–2449).
The Church teaches that work is for the person, and that creation is a gift to be shared and protected (CCC 2426–2436, 2415–2418).
Social teaching is not partisan. It challenges every ideology.
quiz: Rerum Novarum was written by…|Paul VI|Francis|Leo XIII|Pius XII|2|History.
The common good is…|Conditions that let all flourish|Law only|Wealth|The majority wish|0|CCC 1906.
Solidarity means…|Competition|Charity only|Isolation|Sharing burdens|3|CCC 1939.
lessons.life: Do one act of solidarity.
lessons.saint: Dorothy Day: a journalist who founded the Catholic Worker movement to serve the poor.
misc: “Social teaching is just politics.”
“Charity is enough; justice is not the Church’s business.”
lessons.mem: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” (Luke 4:18)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 4:18–19. Ask: “What does ‘good news to the poor’ mean in practice?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name four principles and apply two to a case.

lessons.title: The Church worldwide
lessons.idea: The Catholic Church includes 24 self-governing Churches in full communion with the Pope: the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic Churches. They share one faith and sacraments but have their own liturgies, laws and traditions. Revelation 7:9 pictures every nation worshiping together.
lessons.question: How many Churches are in communion?
lessons.activity: “Churches on a map” (30 min). Students mark the Latin Church and several Eastern Catholic Churches (Maronite, Melkite, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Syro-Malabar, Chaldean, Coptic, Armenian) on a world map. Add one distinctive feature each (liturgical language, icons, married clergy, chrismation of infants).
teach: The Church is catholic in her unity and diversity (CCC 830–838). The Eastern Catholic Churches use the Byzantine, Alexandrian, Antiochene, Armenian and Chaldean rites (CCC 1200–1206).
Many Eastern Catholic Churches ordain married men to the priesthood; infants receive Baptism, Chrismation and Communion together (CCC 1290, 1233).
Eastern Orthodox Churches are not in full communion but share much. Learning from them enriches our faith.
Visit an Eastern Catholic parish if possible.
talk: Why do we have many rites?
quiz: The Church has…|One rite|Many rites in one faith|Two rites|No rites|1|CCC 1203.
Eastern Catholics are led by…|Rome only|Their own bishops united with Rome|Nobody|Kings|1|CCC 882.
The Divine Liturgy is the Eastern name for…|The Mass|Marriage|Baptism|Confession|0|Tradition.
lessons.life: Visit an Eastern Catholic church or watch a Divine Liturgy.
lessons.saint: Josaphat Kuntsevych: a Ruthenian archbishop and martyr who worked for unity between East and West.
misc: “Catholic means Roman Catholic only.”
“Eastern Catholics are Orthodox who converted.”
lessons.mem: “After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages.” (Revelation 7:9)
lessons.hook: Display the Sign of the Cross in different languages or rites. Ask: “Is it the same prayer?” Explore unity in diversity.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name five Churches, their rite and one distinctive practice.

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit in the Church
lessons.idea: The Holy Spirit is the soul of the Church. He sanctifies her, teaches her all truth, gives her gifts and charisms, and unites her to Christ. Jesus promised the Spirit as Advocate and Spirit of truth.
lessons.question: How do we see the Spirit?
lessons.activity: “Study Pentecost and beyond” (30 min). Read Acts 2 and John 14–16. Students chart the Spirit’s work: teaches, recalls Jesus’ words, convicts of sin, guides to truth, empowers witnesses. Add examples from Church history (councils, saints) and personal life.
teach: The Spirit is “the soul of the Church” (CCC 797–798). He builds up the Body through the sacraments, the Word, charisms and ministries (CCC 799–801).
Jesus promised, “He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). The Spirit guides the Church’s Magisterium (CCC 91–93).
Charisms are special graces for the good of the Church (1 Corinthians 12; CCC 799–801). They must be discerned and ordered by pastors.
Teach epiclesis: the Church calls on the Spirit at every sacrament (CCC 1105–1109).
talk: What is the soul of the Church?
How do you see the Spirit?
quiz: The soul of the Church is…|The Holy Spirit|The Pope|The building|The saints|0|CCC 797.
The Spirit gives…|Land|Money|Power|Gifts and charisms|3|CCC 799.
The Spirit teaches…|Violence|Silence|Fear|All truth|3|John 16:13.
lessons.life: Pray Veni Creator.
lessons.saint: Peter: a fisherman who denied Jesus and was forgiven, and became the first pope.
misc: “The Spirit works only in emotional experiences.”
“Only a few are given the Spirit.”
lessons.mem: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things.” (John 14:26)
lessons.hook: Read John 14:16–17. Ask: “What does ‘Advocate’ mean?” (someone called alongside to help). The Spirit never leaves the Church.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe three ways the Spirit acts in the Church.

lessons.title: The gifts and fruits
lessons.idea: Isaiah names seven gifts of the Spirit (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord). Paul lists the fruits (love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control and others). The gifts are given, the fruits ripen.
lessons.question: What are they?
lessons.activity: “Memorize and apply” (30 min). Students memorize the seven gifts and the fruits. Then play a matching game: scenarios (a hard decision, bullying, a test) with the gift that helps. Pray the Veni Creator or Come Holy Spirit.
teach: The seven gifts (Isaiah 11:1–3) make us docile to the Spirit’s promptings (CCC 1830–1831). Wisdom and understanding perfect faith, counsel and fortitude guide action, knowledge helps us see things as God does, piety deepens love and reverence, fear of the Lord is wonder and awe.
The fruits of the Spirit are “the first fruits of eternal glory” (CCC 1832): charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, generosity, gentleness, faithfulness, modesty, self-control, chastity.
Gifts are received at Baptism and strengthened in Confirmation. Fruits show the Spirit at work.
Distinguish gifts from charisms and from virtues.
talk: How do gifts differ from fruits?
quiz: There are…|Three gifts|Twelve gifts|Seven gifts|Nine gifts|2|CCC 1831.
Fortitude is…|Counsel|Courage|Knowledge|Wisdom|1|CCC 1831.
A fruit of the Spirit is…|Joy|Anger|Pride|Fear|0|Galatians 5:22.
lessons.life: Pray daily for one gift.
lessons.saint: Philip Neri: the joyful “apostle of Rome,” who gathered young people for prayer and service.
misc: “Fear of the Lord means being terrified.”
“Gifts are for the holy; fruits are optional.”
lessons.mem: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)
lessons.hook: Show a fruit tree. Ask: “How do you know what kind of tree it is?” By its fruit. Read Galatians 5:22–23.
lessons.assess: Ask students to recite the seven gifts and give an example of a fruit in daily life.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Confirmation
lessons.idea: Confirmation completes baptismal grace. The bishop anoints the forehead with chrism and says, “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” We are strengthened, bound more closely to the Church, and sent to bear witness.
lessons.question: What happens?
lessons.activity: “Prepare the rite” (35 min). Walk through the rite: presentation of candidates, homily, renewal of baptismal promises, laying on of hands, anointing with chrism, general intercessions. Students write what they will say in their own words, and prepare a service project.
teach: Confirmation, with Baptism and the Eucharist, completes initiation (CCC 1285). It imprints an indelible spiritual mark and increases the gifts of the Spirit (CCC 1302–1305).
The essential rite is anointing with chrism, together with the words (CCC 1300). In the Latin Church, the bishop is the ordinary minister (CCC 1312–1314).
Effects: deeper rootedness in divine sonship, closer union with Christ, increase of the Spirit’s gifts, a more perfect bond with the Church, strength to witness (CCC 1303).
Requirements: to be baptized, in a state of grace, with proper instruction. A sponsor accompanies the candidate (CCC 1307–1311).
quiz: Confirmation is a sacrament of…|Marriage|Initiation|Healing|Service|1|CCC 1212.
The anointing is with…|Chrism|Salt|Water|Incense|0|CCC 1297.
A sponsor…|Judges|Pays|Helps the candidate|Replaces the priest|2|CCC 1311.
lessons.life: Write a letter to the bishop asking for Confirmation.
lessons.saint: Philip Neri: the joyful “apostle of Rome,” who gathered young people for prayer and service.
misc: “Confirmation is when I choose to be Catholic.”
“I can skip Confirmation and still be fully initiated.”
lessons.mem: Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit. (Rite of Confirmation)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you need to be ready for a big responsibility?” (training, support, strength). Confirmation is God’s strengthening.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the rite, its effects and what it asks of them.

units.title: Living a moral life
units.eq: How do we live as disciples?

lessons.title: Conscience and freedom
lessons.idea: Freedom is not doing whatever we want but the power to choose the good. Conscience is the inner judgment that helps us see what is right, and it must be formed. True freedom grows as we practice virtue.
lessons.question: What is freedom?
lessons.activity: “Case study debate” (35 min). Present cases (peer pressure to cheat, a rumor, a risky dare, honesty about a mistake). Students apply the steps of conscience: pray, learn what the Church teaches, seek advice, weigh consequences, choose. Discuss which choices lead to freedom.
teach: Freedom is “the power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that” (CCC 1731). It grows to perfection when directed to God (CCC 1731, 1744). “For freedom Christ has set us free” (Galatians 5:1).
The human act is judged by its object, intention and circumstances (CCC 1750–1756). A good intention does not make a bad act good.
Conscience must be formed; one is obliged to follow a certain conscience (CCC 1776–1785). Ignorance may lessen responsibility, but we should seek the truth.
Freedom is limited by habits, fear and social pressure, but never destroyed (CCC 1735–1748).
quiz: Freedom is…|Having money|Power to choose the good|Avoiding rules|Doing anything|1|CCC 1731.
Conscience must be…|Silent|Hidden|Formed|Ignored|2|CCC 1783.
A person must always follow…|A friend|The crowd|Feeling|A certain judgment of conscience|3|CCC 1790.
lessons.life: Examine a decision with the Church’s teaching.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: the lawyer and statesman who told the truth to a king and died for his conscience.
misc: “Freedom is doing what I want.”
“If I feel good about it, my conscience is clear.”
lessons.mem: “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore.” (Galatians 5:1)
lessons.hook: Present two images: a train on tracks and a train off the tracks. “Which is free to go where it was made to go?” Freedom is for something.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain true freedom and the steps of forming a conscience with an example.

lessons.title: Virtue and sin
lessons.idea: Virtue builds the good; sin harms. Virtues are habits that make doing good easier. The capital sins — pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth — are root vices. The remedy is grace and daily practice.
lessons.question: How do we grow?
lessons.activity: “Growth plan” (30 min). Each student identifies one virtue to grow and the opposing vice, plans three daily practices, a support (friend, prayer, sacrament) and a way to track progress. Read Romans 7:15–25 as a sign that struggle is normal.
teach: Virtue is a firm disposition to do good (CCC 1803). Human virtues are acquired; theological virtues are gifts (CCC 1804–1829).
Sin is an offense against God, reason and truth (CCC 1849). It creates a tendency to more sin (vice). The capital sins give rise to others (CCC 1866).
Romans 7: “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” Paul shows both struggle and hope: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ.”
Address both pride and scrupulosity. God’s grace strengthens; examine yourself without despair.
quiz: Capital sins are…|Imaginary|Venial sins only|Greatest crimes|Sources of other sins|3|CCC 1866.
A virtue is…|A feeling|A good habit|A thought|A rule|1|CCC 1803.
Pride is…|Disordered love of self|Courage|Joy|Humility|0|CCC 1866.
lessons.life: Choose a virtue to oppose a vice.
lessons.saint: Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
misc: “I can overcome all sin by willpower.”
“Everyone sins, so it doesn’t matter.”
lessons.mem: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does an athlete do to become strong?” Daily practice. The same is true for virtues; vice is a habit too.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the seven capital sins with their opposing virtues.

lessons.title: Respect for life and the person
lessons.idea: Every human life is sacred from conception to natural death because each person is made in God’s image. The fifth commandment forbids murder, abortion, euthanasia and suicide, and calls us to protect life and care for the vulnerable.
lessons.question: Why life?
lessons.activity: “Service project” (35 min). Plan a project that honors life: visit a nursing home, help a pro-life pregnancy center, make cards for the sick, write to a lonely person. Prepare respectfully and discuss how to speak with charity about hard topics.
teach: Human life is sacred (CCC 2258). Direct and intentional killing of an innocent person is gravely wrong (CCC 2268–2269). Abortion is a grave offense (CCC 2270–2275).

Euthanasia and assisted suicide are morally unacceptable; legitimate refusal of burdensome treatment is allowed (CCC 2276–2279). Suicide is contrary to love of self and God, though the Church prays for those who die this way (CCC 2280–2283).
The Church also protects life by defending the poor, the immigrant, the prisoner, and by promoting peace (CCC 2302–2317). The death penalty is now judged inadmissible (CCC 2267).
Offer compassion to women facing difficult pregnancies and to those who have suffered abortion or loss; Project Rachel offers healing.
talk: What does the Church teach about the dying?
quiz: Human life is sacred from…|Age 5|Conception to natural death|Age 18|Birth|1|CCC 2270.
The Church teaches that euthanasia is…|Optional|A right|Fine|Morally unacceptable|3|CCC 2277.
We should care for…|Nobody|The powerful|The famous|The poor and the weak|3|CCC 2448.
lessons.life: Support a pro-life ministry.
lessons.saint: Gianna Molla: a doctor and mother who chose her baby’s life over her own.
misc: “The Church cares about life only before birth.”
“All end-of-life care must be continued.”
lessons.mem: “For you formed my inward parts; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.” (Psalm 139:13)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 139:13–16 aloud. Ask: “What does this say about how God sees each of us before anyone else does?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the dignity of life and two ways to protect it.

units.title: Prayer and mission
units.eq: How do we live our faith?

lessons.title: Ways of praying
lessons.idea: Prayer takes three main expressions: vocal prayer with words, meditation with thought, and contemplation, a silent gaze of love. All three have a place in a mature life of prayer.
lessons.question: What is your method?
lessons.activity: “Try three forms” (35 min). Stations: vocal (pray the Our Father slowly), meditation (read Matthew 6:25–34 and imagine the scene), contemplation (sit with the Jesus Prayer: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me”). Students write a brief reflection after each.
teach: Vocal prayer unites body and spirit; Jesus taught us the Our Father (CCC 2700–2704). Meditation seeks to understand the why and how of the Christian life (CCC 2705–2708).
Contemplative prayer is “a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus… a silent love” (CCC 2709–2719). It is a gift, not a technique.
Obstacles: distraction, dryness, acedia (CCC 2729–2733). Remedies: persevering, humility, simple trust.
Encourage a daily rhythm: morning offering, mealtime, a quiet ten minutes, examen at night.
quiz: Vocal prayer uses…|Silence|Dance|Art|Words|3|CCC 2700.
Meditation is…|Daydreaming|Seeking understanding|Reading news|Napping|1|CCC 2705.
Contemplation is…|Singing|Silent love|Argument|Math|1|CCC 2709.
lessons.life: Try 3 minutes of silent prayer daily.
lessons.saint: Teresa: a Carmelite who reformed her order and taught that prayer is friendship with God.
misc: “If my mind wanders, I’m failing.”
“Meditation means emptying my mind.”
lessons.mem: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” (The Jesus Prayer)
lessons.hook: Say the Jesus Prayer slowly for one minute in silence. Ask what they noticed. Introduce the three expressions.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe each expression of prayer and which they will practice this week.

lessons.title: The Mass and Adoration
lessons.idea: The Eucharist feeds us as the bread of life, and Eucharistic adoration extends the Mass by prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. Jesus said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”
lessons.question: Why adoration?
lessons.activity: “Visit the Blessed Sacrament” (30 min). Take students to church for a silent visit. Teach how to genuflect, kneel and pray: adoration, thanksgiving, sorrow, petition (ACTS). Afterwards, write a prayer and share what struck them.
teach: The Eucharist is the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of Christ (CCC 1374). In John 6 Jesus says his flesh is “true food” (John 6:55) and many disciples left rather than accept it.
Eucharistic worship outside Mass is a prolongation of Mass (CCC 1378–1381). The tabernacle, Benediction and Forty Hours devotion honor Christ present.
The fruits of Communion: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, protection from mortal sin, unity of the Church (CCC 1391–1397).
Teach the Church’s norms of preparation and reverence (CCC 1385–1389).
quiz: Adoration is…|Magic|Habit|Worship of Christ in the Eucharist|Worship of bread|2|CCC 1378.
The Blessed Sacrament is kept in the…|Sacristy|Pew|Chalice|Tabernacle|3|CCC 1379.
Benediction ends with…|Homily|Gloria|A blessing|Creed|2|Tradition.
lessons.life: Spend 15 minutes in adoration.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a teenager who loved the Eucharist, used computers to share the faith and died at 15.
misc: “Adoration is staring at bread.”
“Communion is optional if I go to Mass.”
lessons.mem: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.” (John 6:51)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does food do?” (feeds, strengthens, shares). Read John 6:35 and 6:51 and note what Jesus says about himself as food.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Real Presence and how adoration relates to Mass.

lessons.title: Called to evangelize
lessons.idea: Every baptized Catholic shares in the Church’s mission to evangelize. We witness by how we live and by what we say, with respect and joy. Evangelization begins with a personal encounter with Jesus.
lessons.question: How will you witness?
lessons.activity: “Witness project” (35 min). Students write a 30-second testimony (“how God has been present to me”), then plan a witness project: a service day, inviting a friend to Mass, a social media post, or a prayer group. Practice with partners.
teach: Evangelization means proclaiming the Gospel to bring people to Christ (CCC 849–856, 863). All the baptized share in this mission through their baptismal priesthood (CCC 900, 905).
The Church teaches that mission respects freedom (CCC 160, 2104–2109). Pope Francis stresses that the Church grows by attraction, not proclaiming at others.

Witness of life, loving service and clear explanation work together. “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence” (1 Peter 3:15).
Mention the new evangelization, called for by John Paul II.
quiz: All the baptized are called to…|Rule|Rest|Evangelize|Hide|2|CCC 905.
Evangelization is…|Shaming|Debating|Winning|Sharing the Good News|3|CCC 853.
The mission is rooted in…|Money|Culture|Politics|Christ’s command|3|Matthew 28:19.
lessons.life: Share your faith in one concrete way.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit missionary who carried the Gospel to India and Japan.
misc: “Evangelization is only for missionaries.”
“Evangelization means arguing people into the Church.”
lessons.mem: “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you.” (1 Peter 3:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If someone asked why you believe, what would you say in 30 seconds?” Then read Matthew 28:19–20 and 1 Peter 3:15.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state their testimony and one concrete witness step.

units.title: Hard questions: faith, science and history
units.eq: Can I trust a Church that has made mistakes?

lessons.title: Genesis, evolution and the big bang
lessons.idea: Faith and science are both ways of seeking truth, so they cannot truly contradict each other. Genesis teaches why the world exists, not how it works.
lessons.question: Does science disprove the Bible?
lessons.activity: Write two columns: the questions science answers and the questions Genesis answers.
teach: The Church teaches that God created everything and that faith and reason cannot contradict (CCC 159). The Church has not defined how God brought about living things; it teaches that the human soul is created directly by God (CCC 366).

Catholics may accept the big bang and evolution. Fr. Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, proposed the big bang theory. Pope Pius XII (Humani Generis, 1950) and St John Paul II (1996) said evolution is not opposed to faith.
The Church reads Genesis for its truths about God, creation, the goodness of the world, the dignity of man and the fall (CCC 289, 337, 390), as sacred writers used stories to teach.
Not every Christian reads Genesis this way. Be kind to classmates who see it differently, and teach what the Church teaches.
talk: What questions does science answer best? What questions can it not answer?
Why might someone think faith and science must fight?
What do the first pages of Genesis teach about the world even if they are not a science book?
quiz: Who proposed the big bang theory?|A Catholic priest, Georges Lemaître|Pope Pius IX|Galileo|Charles Darwin|0|He was a Belgian priest and physicist.
What does the Church teach about the human soul?|It is created directly by God|It is not part of the person|It is a product of the brain only|It evolves from animal souls|0|CCC 366.
Faith and science, rightly understood…|Must always be opposed|Never speak of the same world|Are the same thing|Cannot contradict each other|3|CCC 159.
lessons.life: Ask a science teacher what question first made them curious. Pray a psalm of wonder (Psalm 8).
lessons.saint: Albert the Great: a Dominican who studied plants, animals and stars and taught that nature and faith belong together.
misc: “The Church says you cannot believe in evolution.”
“Science has proved there is no God.”
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where did you first hear that you have to choose between faith and science?” Take a few answers, then say that the Church has never taught that.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what Genesis 1 teaches and what questions science answers.

lessons.title: Galileo, the Inquisition and the Crusades
lessons.idea: The Church is holy, but its members are sinners. The Church admits real wrongs and tries to tell the truth about its past.
lessons.question: Can the Church be holy if its people do wrong?
lessons.activity: Write a fair summary of one event from two points of view.
teach: The Church is holy because of Christ and the Holy Spirit, but it is made of sinners, and it is always in need of purification (CCC 823, 827). Jesus said the weeds grow with the wheat until the harvest (Matthew 13).

Galileo was tried in 1633 for teaching that the earth moves; in 1992 St John Paul II said the judges had made a mistake. The story is more complicated than “religion against science”: many church leaders and scientists were Catholics.

The Crusades and the Inquisition included real violence and injustice. On March 12, 2000 St John Paul II asked forgiveness for the sins of the Church’s children, including violence in the service of truth.
Be wary of both myths: “the Church has done nothing wrong” and “the Church has only done wrong.” Look at the sources.
talk: Why is it harder to say sorry for what a group did than for what I did?
What is the difference between the Church’s teaching and the actions of some of its members?
Why does the truth about the past matter?
quiz: In 1992 Pope John Paul II said about Galileo’s trial that…|Galileo was a heretic|The judges made a mistake|Galileo had been right about everything and the Church had never made an error|The Church should never admit errors|1|He recognized the error.
The Church is called holy because…|The pope is sinless|Its members never sin|Its history has no failures|Christ and the Holy Spirit make it holy, though its members are sinners|3|CCC 823, 827.
What did Pope John Paul II do on March 12, 2000?|Closed the Vatican Library|Ended the Inquisition|Asked forgiveness for the sins of the Church’s children|Canceled the Jubilee|2|The Day of Pardon.
lessons.life: Read a short, fair article about one historical event and share one thing you learned.
lessons.saint: Bartolomé de las Casas: a priest who spoke out against the abuse of Native peoples in the Americas.
misc: “The Church burned Galileo at the stake.”
“If members of the Church did wrong, the Church cannot be true.”
lessons.mem: “Let both grow together until the harvest.” (Matthew 13:30)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is it harder to admit a family member’s mistake or your own?” Frame the lesson as honest history from people who love the Church.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe one event from two points of view and say what the Church has acknowledged.

lessons.title: Why does a good God allow suffering?
lessons.idea: God does not will evil, yet allows it for a greater good. In Christ he enters suffering and brings life from it.
lessons.question: If God is good, why is there suffering?
lessons.activity: Write a letter to someone who is hurting.
teach: The Catechism asks the question plainly (CCC 309). There is no single answer; the whole of faith is the answer (CCC 309). God is not the author of evil, and he permits it only to bring a greater good (CCC 311–312).
Some suffering comes from human freedom and sin, some from a world still unfinished (CCC 310). Jesus did not explain suffering away. He shared it, died, and rose.
The right first response to someone suffering is love and presence, not an argument. Job’s friends were wrong when they explained too quickly.
Christians are called to relieve suffering (works of mercy) and to unite their own to Christ (CCC 1521).
talk: Have you ever been helped by someone who just stayed beside you?
Why do arguments often fail a hurting person?
What does the cross tell us about God and suffering?
quiz: Does God cause evil?|He has no power over it|He does not know about it|Yes, to teach lessons|No, he permits it for a greater good|3|CCC 311.
In the book of Job, the friends who explain Job’s suffering as punishment are…|Healed|Praised|Rebuked by God|Ignored|2|Job 42:7.
What does the Catechism say is the answer to the problem of evil?|No answer exists|A single short argument|The whole of the Christian faith|Only science|2|CCC 309.
lessons.life: Visit, call or write to someone who is suffering this week.
lessons.saint: Josephine Bakhita: born into slavery in Sudan, she became a Canossian sister and said she would thank her captors because suffering led her to Christ.
misc: “God sends suffering to punish us for specific sins.”
“If God loved us, nothing bad would ever happen.”
lessons.mem: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that many students have faced pain. Invite quiet before beginning, and give permission to step out.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state what the Church teaches about God and evil and one way to accompany someone who suffers.

units.title: Justice, truth and contentment
units.eq: How do we love our neighbor in what we have and what we say?

lessons.title: You shall not steal: justice and respect for goods
lessons.idea: The seventh commandment forbids stealing and cheating and asks us to be fair, honest and generous. God gave the earth to everyone, so we share what we have and care for the poor.
lessons.question: What do justice and generosity ask of us?
lessons.activity: Role-play cases: found money, borrowed items, pirated media, unfair work. Decide what justice requires and how to repair harm.
teach: “You shall not steal” protects the goods of others (CCC 2401–2414). Theft, fraud, cheating, unjust wages and pirating are sins. Restitution repairs the wrong (CCC 2412).
The earth’s goods are meant for everyone, so private property has a social purpose (CCC 2402–2406). Giving to the poor is an act of justice (CCC 2446).
We care for creation and animals (CCC 2415–2418). John the Baptist told soldiers and tax collectors to be fair (Luke 3:10–14).
Be mindful that students may face poverty. Never shame.
talk: When is it hard to be honest about money or things?
How do you repair a wrong?
What can we do for people with less?
quiz: Restitution means…|Hiding it|Repairing what was taken|Blaming|Forgetting|1|CCC 2412.
The goods of the earth are meant for…|Everyone|A few|Kings|Nobody|0|CCC 2402.

lessons.title: You shall not bear false witness: truth and trust
lessons.idea: The eighth commandment asks us to speak the truth in love. Lies, gossip, rash judgment and betraying secrets harm trust. Jesus is the Truth.
lessons.question: Why does truth matter so much?
lessons.activity: Sort statements into truth, gossip, lies, calumny, detraction, rash judgment. Write a short, kind way to say a hard truth.
teach: Jesus is the Truth (John 14:6). We bear witness to him by truthful speech and sometimes at great cost, as martyrs do (CCC 2464–2474).
Sins against truth: lying, perjury, rash judgment, detraction, calumny, flattery (CCC 2475–2487). Reparation includes correcting the record.
Secrets and privacy are to be respected; the seal of Confession is absolute (CCC 2488–2492). Media and social networks call for honesty and charity (CCC 2493–2499).
Truth must be spoken with love: “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15).
talk: When is it hard to tell the truth?
What is the difference between gossip and concern?
How do we handle truth online?

lessons.life: Choose to speak only what is true and kind for a day, and make amends where you gossiped.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: he refused to lie under oath and died for the truth.
misc: “White lies don’t matter.”
“Truth should be used as a weapon.”
lessons.mem: “Let your yes be yes and your no be no.” (Matthew 5:37)
lessons.hook: Play “telephone” with a short sentence and compare the end. Ask what happens to trust when words change.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define lying, detraction and calumny and give a repair for each.

lessons.title: You shall not covet: freedom of heart
lessons.idea: The ninth and tenth commandments reach into the heart: purity of heart and freedom from envy and greed. Gratitude, generosity and trust in God make us free.
lessons.question: How do we keep a heart free of envy?
lessons.activity: Write a gratitude list of ten things you have. Then draw a “heart garden” with plants that stand for gratitude, generosity and trust.
teach: The ninth commandment protects purity of heart (CCC 2514–2533). Jesus says, “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matthew 5:8). Purity needs prayer, modesty and discipline of the senses.
The tenth guards against greed and envy (CCC 2534–2557). Envy is sadness at another’s good; it is a capital sin (CCC 2538–2540).
The remedy is gratitude, humility and trust in providence. “Where your treasure is, there will be your heart also” (Matthew 6:21; CCC 2544–2547).
Teach with compassion. Social media can inflame comparison; invite students to notice it.
talk: How can gratitude change how we see things?
What does a pure heart look like?

lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the ninth and tenth commandments and a practice that helps.
